blocks.title: Schmitt Trigger
blocks.body: A comparator circuit with positive feedback that exhibits hysteresis. Unlike a simple comparator, the Schmitt trigger switches thresholds depending on the current output state, preventing multiple triggering caused by input noise.

blocks.caption: Inverting Schmitt trigger with resistive positive feedback network

blocks.title: Upper and Lower Switching Thresholds
blocks.note: Assuming symmetric saturation voltages $\pm V_\mathrm{sat}$, the hysteresis window width is $V_H = V_{TH} - V_{TL} = \frac{2 R_1}{R_1 + R_2} V_\mathrm{sat}$.

blocks.title: Symmetric Hysteresis Design
blocks.body: With rail voltages providing $V_\mathrm{sat} = \pm 12\,\mathrm{V}$, choosing $R_1 = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ and $R_2 = 90\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ yields a feedback factor $\beta = \frac{10}{10+90} = 0.1$. The switching thresholds are $V_{TH} = +1.2\,\mathrm{V}$ and $V_{TL} = -1.2\,\mathrm{V}$, yielding a noise margin hysteresis width of $V_H = 2.4\,\mathrm{V}$.

blocks.title: Op-Amp Slew Rate & Recovery
blocks.body: Because the op-amp operates in full saturation, recovery time from saturation adds delay. For high-frequency waveform generation or fast clock recovery, use a dedicated comparator IC (e.g. LM311 or LM393) rather than a general-purpose op-amp.

points: Positive feedback to the non-inverting terminal creates bistable operation and hysteresis.
Noise within the hysteresis band $V_H$ cannot trigger spurious transitions.
Inverting topology means an input exceeding $V_{TH}$ forces the output to its negative rail.

questions: How can the hysteresis center be shifted away from 0 V to create an asymmetric threshold?
Why does negative feedback linearize while positive feedback creates bistability?
